utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I raise one matter before the witness comes in. There is an application to revise the Rule 65 ter list and add a number of witnesses and remove a number. The Chamber has decided on the action to take, which largely grants the motion. There's just one exception. But one of the issues that arises is in relation to a witness Sterenberg.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I may have the wrong name. One of the witnesses is scheduled for next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It is --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The name is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It is Sterenberg. The Chamber's decision is to allow that witness to be added, and there will be a written decision filed either later today or tomorrow. We need to know, however, whether calling him next week will cause difficulty for the Defence or whether knowing now that the Chamber is going to allow the witness to give evidence he can be taken next week. Now, can you tell me whether there would be difficulty dealing with his evidence if he were called next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we inform you at the first break? After the first break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. If it does - and we're relying on your judgement on this - then we will order that he does not give evidence until at least the middle of January. But if you can accommodate the situation, knowing that that's the decision of the Chamber in any event, to allow him, then obviously that would be extremely helpful to the progress of the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, one of the witnesses, the reasons why he was brought forward was because there are indications that he might be completely unavailable or likely to be unavailable next year, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This isn't a matter for debate, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have made our minds up. We only need to know whether that's going to cause difficulty for the Defence or whether they can accommodate the situation. We can now have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Cvetic. Your examination by Mr. Stamp will now continue. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Cvetic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I would just like to run very quickly through the organisation of the MUP, particularly as it relates to Kosovo and the personnel thereof --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be moved closer to the microphone, please, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- of a SUP, S-U-P, for Kosovska Mitrovica. Can you just tell us briefly or describe briefly the role and function of the SUPs within the organisation of police services in Serbia in the latter part of 1997, 1998, 1999.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the level of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia, and in keeping with the law on internal affairs, the minister of the interior of the Republic of Serbia put into force a rule book or rules of procedure on the internal organisation of the Ministry of the Interior. In the rule book, what is foreseen is to have 33 SUPs which were supposed to be internal organisational units of the Ministry of the Interior. In the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, there was a total of seven, Pristina, Gnjilane, Urosevac, Prizren, Djakovica, Pec, and Kosovska Mitrovica, each of these places had their own SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What was the territorial jurisdiction of each SUP? Or may I just put it this way: Were the SUPs responsible for the municipality of police affairs in one or more than one municipality within Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try and be specific. This SUP of Kosovska Mitrovica included the area of the Kosovska Mitrovica district comprising the following municipalities: The municipality of Kosovska Mitrovica, then the municipality of Leposavic, Zvecan, Zubin Potok, Vucitrn, and Srbica. As for the other secretariats, I don't have such specific data.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But in respect to the other secretariats, they would also be responsible for the management of the affairs in various municipalities within Kosovo? Each SUP was allocated a group of municipalities to manage. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, within the organisation or the administration of the police in Serbia and in Kosovo and Metohija, which police organ were the SUPs subordinated to, to whom did they report administratively?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The secretariats of internal affairs in Kosovo and Metohija were directly under the Ministry of the Interior and the MUP headquarters or staff in Pristina. They reported to the MUP staff in Pristina and the Ministry of the Interior in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the Ministry of the Interior in Belgrade, would that be the RJB, the public security department?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to the public security department. Anything which fell under the work of the public security department had to do with public security in general. In Kosovo there was separate units as well as in Serbia which were tasked to work on state security. The secretariats had the sole role within the domain of public security.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown exhibit P1072, please. And, Your Honours, I just want the witness to identify the document. It is a legal document and I think it can be agreed upon later on what it is and it will be discussed by another witness. But pending that agreement, perhaps the witness could just identify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Does that document there contain the rules which govern the internal -- the establishment and the internal organisation of the SUPs?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, the minister of the interior, pursuant to the law on internal affairs, put this into force. I don't know exactly which article of the law it includes; I believe it is Article 6. Based on that, he put these rules into force on the internal organisation of the Ministry of the Interior. And an excerpt of the rules was forwarded to each of the secretariats in Serbia and in Kosovo and Metohija. Before me, I see its title page: "Rules establishing the internal organisation of the Ministry of the Interior for the SUP Pristina." Such rules were forwarded to each of the secretariats in Kosovo and in Serbia, the total being 33.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in respect to the organs and bodies that were subordinated to the SUPs, there were also departments of internal affairs, were there not; and if so, could you just briefly describe the role and function of these departments?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Each secretariat for internal affairs in Serbia and in Kosovo and Metohija had its own subunits, organisationally speaking. They were termed OUPs, the departments of internal affairs and police stations. To be specific, the SUP of Kosovska Mitrovica had a OUP in Vucitrn, in Srbica, in Leposavic. And they had a police station in Zvecani and another one in Zubin Potok. A similar type of organisation could be found in the other SUPs in Kosovo and Serbia, depending on the security assessment which had to be carried out previously. If need be, I can explain the internal organisation of the OUPs as to what they comprised and what fell within individual police stations as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. The police stations and the OUPs were manned by regular police personnel. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By a decree of the systematisation of the Ministry of the Interior, which was forwarded to all the secretariats, job descriptions were provided describing the level of education and experience needed to carry out specific tasks and duties. There was a systematic table for all job descriptions in police stations and OUPs, and there were regular employees manning such stations and OUPs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And were the regular police or the regular employees manning the OUPs and the police station augmented - and I'm speaking particularly now in 1998 and 1999 in Kosovo and Metohija - were they augmented by the recruitment or the enlistment of reserve police officers?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In keeping with the law on internal affairs, in order to carry out tasks pertaining to internal affairs, one can employ or recruit people from the reserve force as well. Such a decision needs to be made by the Minister of the Interior, and pursuant to the same law, he issued a directive on the type of work within the police tasked with -- which can be carried out by reservists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cvetic, what is the difference in -- in an area between an OUP and a police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The OUP is the department of internal affairs. Each OUP had a police station as well as several other organisational units, whereas an individual police station is a unit in itself and nothing else. The other smaller organisational units which fell under various OUPs is something I can explain further in detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It probably won't be necessary. That was very helpful. Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How many reservists were enlisted in the MUP or the -- or your -- your secretariat, the secretariat for Kosovska Mitrovica, in 1998?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the police reserve force were used at certain points during 1998 on various tasks. The maximum number of such reservists at a given point equalled the number of those on active duty; the ratio was one-to-one, and it only happened when the security situation demanded such a ratio to be in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And in the early part -- in 1998, can you recall approximately how many reservists there were in your SUP?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some 665 reservists, and the same number goes for the active officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, in 1999, particularly in March 1999, did this number remain the same or were there efforts made to increase the number?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Upon completion of anti-terrorist actions undertaken in Kosovo and Metohija between the 25th of July and the 29th of September, 1998, and once the OSCE mission arrived and after the Milosevic-Holbrooke agreement was signed, it was agreed that the number of the police in place in Kosovo to be reduced. In Kosovo as a whole, there were 14.571 policemen. By virtue of the agreement the figure was brought down to 10.021. In early 1999, when terrorist activities were stepped up, another mobilisation was carried out recruiting both active and reserve policemen. When I say "active policemen" it included members of police special units, which had been withdrawn once the OSCE mission arrived. And later, in March, immediately prior to the aggression, they were again grouped in the area of Kosovo. The mobilisation was ordered on the 17th of March and was supposed to be completed by the 20th of March, 1999. The number of police in Kosovo was between 14.500 and 15.000. In the SUP in Kosovska Mitrovica, there were policemen from the special -- with the PJP, and the number was 1.099 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the end of his answer. He mentioned two figures which the interpreters did not catch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: At the end of your answer you gave us two figures there, one of them was 1.099. What was the other figure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Kosovska Mitrovica there were 1.999 and not 1.099.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is 1.999 policemen, some of whom were members of the PJP. Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I understood it rather differently from that. You mean including PJP who were not normally based in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Later on after the mobilisation, between the 17th and 20th of March, they were sent to the area of Kosovo since an imminent threat of war was proclaimed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The regular police, I take it, would have been trained and paid and disciplined within the normal police framework. So I'd like to just ask you a couple of questions about the reservists, reserve police. How many of them were there by March 1999 in Kosovo and how many in your SUP?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the ratio between the active and reserve police members was one-to-one. According to the job description schedule, there were 665 active policemen and the number of reservists was the same. What you, however, probably have in mind are the reserve police detachments which were formed. As for those, they were formed in June 1998 in order to defend villages against terrorist attacks and in order to protect the population. At that time, terrorist activities increased, they made incursions into villages, they robbed, looted, and took away property and vehicles. Therefore, a decision was made for every village in Kosovo and Metohija to have reserve police detachments to protect such settlements from terrorist gangs' incursions. In the area of Kosovska Mitrovica, there was a total of 58 reserve police detachments; in Kosovo as a whole, there were 254. Such detachments comprised local inhabitants, people who lived there and worked there, and they were used as needed. They were armed, and their total number was around 2.000 in Kosovska Mitrovica. As for these reserve police detachments, in the overall structure there were some 6.034 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So if you could just tell me briefly, what was the distinction between members of the reserve police and members of these reserve police detachments, if any?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, members of the reserve force of the police, when they were used in accordance with the law on internal affairs, had all the rights as did the members of the active police force. And when they were not being used, they did not have such rights. As regards the reserve police detachments, the reserve police squads, these squads were armed but they were not completely uniformed because we lacked a number of uniforms. They were organised upon the military principle. They had their commanders or squad leaders and deputy squad leaders, the komandiri, and the necessary number of policemen. They were not remunerated adequately for that, in other words they received no salaries and they did not have the same rights as these reserve police members who would be used in accordance with the provisions of the law on the interior. The reserve police squads also comprised citizens who had a wartime duty station also according to a different obligation. For instance, people who were assigned either to the civil defence or to local units of the Army of Yugoslavia, and their exclusive task was defence of the villages. For that, for their activity, the scope of their competence, of their work, was prescribed by an instruction, a very clear instruction, on the defence of inhabited places which also spelled out the procedure to be followed. This instruction was forwarded to all the secretariats and by all the secretariats to all the units by the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, I don't want us to move away from reserves just now but you mentioned Joint Command. What do you mean when you referred to "Joint Command"?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, during 1998, or more precisely in July 1998, at a meeting in the MUP staff in Pristina, all the heads of secretariats from the area of Kosovo were informed of the fact that a command had been set up at the highest level, its mandate being to integrate the activities of the army and police in the implementation of anti-terrorist operations, which ensued in the coming period, in the period that followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. We return to the Joint Command, but let me finish quickly on the reserve police detachments. The reserve police units -- or the reserve police detachments that were involved in village defence to whom did they or their commanders report within the scheme or the framework of police management in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had their own commander, and he liaised with the commander of the police station in his area and the commander of the police station with the head of the department of the police, i.e., the head of the secretariat of the area in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Who armed them? Who gave them weapons?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reserve police squads were armed from the level of the Ministry of the Interior through the MUP staff in Pristina and the staff MUP did that through the Secretariats of the Interior in the area of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we bring up document P1115.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And while that is coming up, may I just ask you one thing. You said earlier that the reserve police -- members of the reserve police detachments did not have uniforms or full uniforms. Did they have at least a part of a uniform, a police uniform, or were some of them in -- entirely clad in civilian clothes while they were on duty?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can say that they didn't have any part of a police uniform. They had basic equipment of a soldier, which is to say a cap, a jacket, belt, and parts of equipment like that. It -- I don't know that the reserve police squads did not have any equipment. I can say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Again, I would like just to take you back briefly. You were asked about reserve police detachments. Did they or their commanders -- sorry. To whom did they or their commanders report within the scheme or framework of police management in Kosovo? And you said that they had their commander and he liaised with the commander of the police station in his area. Now, what do you mean he liaised with the commander of the police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The reports from their terrain, from their villages were would be submitted by them to the commander of the police station who covered the -- the village in question territory-wise. And the commander of the police station would submit to them certain instructions in terms of the method of carrying out their tasks and the general procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who would decide on the tasks that they had to undertake?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, depending on the security situation and the security issues, decisions would be submitted either from the level of the Ministry of the Interior or the MUP staff in Pristina, the secretariats of the interior, the departments of internal affairs, or police stations as the last, lowest units. Otherwise, in respect of all those reserve police squads, certain documents had been drawn up. First and foremost, instructions on the defence of settlements; then an aide-memoire on the conduct of members of the police when they should find themselves in a zone which was riddled by terrorist groups; and then combat training instructions and instructions also on command liaison communication methods.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you have a look at the document on the screen. This is a memorandum dated 30th of July, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we scroll down to the signature block, please. And you see that's a memorandum from the head of staff, Major-General Sreten Lukic. Is that what you see reflected in the document?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And in the body of the document it refers to weapons issued by the Army of Yugoslavia to citizens engaged in the reserve police stations to defend villages and cities in the municipalities under the jurisdiction of the areas of the secretariats.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we scroll to the next page, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you do that, can you explain to me what a reserve police station is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Reserve police squads, as I've said, were set up to defend inhabited places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's a mistranslation I think. RPO should be reserve police detachment or squad. We need to be -- you need to be careful about this, Mr. Stamp. This is very important evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you read the first paragraph of the memorandum, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And can I just ask the interpreters to interpret it from what is read by the witness and not what is on the translated document. Could you read the first paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Please find enclosed extracts from the register of weapons issued by the Army of Yugoslavia to citizens engaged in reserve police squads to defend villages and cities in the municipalities under your secretariat's jurisdiction."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And could we --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And just to be clear, the reserve police squads referred to there is the same thing that you were discussing earlier as reserve police detachments?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, in the area of Kosovo and Metohija there existed competent military territorial organs. They were the commands of the military OUP boards. These commands according to their plans of use had a number of units that was also set up in the different villages and the commands of the military boards armed those units with automatic and semi-automatic weaponry. Those units which were part of these military districts, rather than boards, if they were not used -- if they were not used for the needs of the military organs, they would be used and engaged as part of the reserve police squads. That is why at the beginning when I talked about how many had been armed within the reserve police squads, I mentioned the figure of 6.034 as the total number and 2.000 was the number in the reserve squads, which there were 58. And the other arms and armaments were issued to other members and to other citizens who were issued arms on different grounds because they had some different obligations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we look at the second page just to see the total number of weapons issued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm glad you understand that, Mr. Stamp. If you just want -- it will not do to throw all this material at us and expect us to sort it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's return to the last answer. There were as well set up in the -- at the village level units which were under the military districts. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And many times when they were not engaged by the military, these citizens in these units would be used, if necessary, for the needs of the police reserve squads?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I've understood that. What I don't understand is what P1115 has got to do with these bodies, these military territorial organs. Are we going to come to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I see. Very well. Carry on then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If you -- the weapons you see --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, could we -- yes, we are there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There's a total number of weapons P43 -- sorry. 7.436. Were these weapons distributed or issued to citizens within your SUP at that time? What the document reflects -- could I just ask to which citizens and on what basis were these weapons distributed?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The citizens would be issued with weapons on the basis of their wartime duty stations under the Law on Defence. Every citizen had certain rights and certain obligations and duties, so that a citizen could be assigned to serve for the needs of the Army of Yugoslavia, for the needs of the military territorial organs, for the needs of the organs of the interior, the police, for the needs of civil defence, for the surveillance of reporting service, for the command liaison communications centre, and for other needs within the defence effort. In this second instance - and I do not see the entire original document right now -- well, yes, now I do see it - that is the number which on the 30th of July featured in the area of Kosovska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Would you be able to say how many of those weapons were distributed to reserve police detachments or citizens who were members of reserve police detachments?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, when you look at just the police -- reserve police squads or detachments, that's about 2.000. But if you take into account the fact that this reserve force also comprises citizens assigned to it on different grounds, then we have this figure, the figure of 7.000 and -- I can't see the rest. 7.436.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we have a look at P0 -- I beg your pardon. P1114.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before we get there, were Kosovo Albanians issued with any of these weapons?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not issued with weapons in a systematic way, in this way. But as citizens, because every citizen, according to the law on arms and ammunition, could apply to be issued permission to buy, to purchase, weapons, meaning hunting weapons and pistols and not soldier's weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The document before you, which is P1114 dated the 1st of July, 1998, can we just quickly go to the last page of the document, it is a document that you signed as head of the secretariat. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we could return to the front, the first page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think you have here that in Kosovska Mitrovica SUP area for the one reserve branch, police stations have been organised. I take it these are reserve police detachments have been organised as a total of 1.374 members. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what this document states, and I've already stressed that in the area of Kosovska Mitrovica there had been organised 58 reserve police detachments, with a total of about 2.000 members. Can I just see the date, yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do we have an English version of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Can we put on the screen the English version of P1114. I think you could split the screen if possible. I'm very sorry, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: While we are getting the two documents on the screen, you were explaining, Mr. Cvetic, the difference in the number of reserve police detachments, and you were referring to the date of the document, which is the 1st of July, 1998. Would you like to briefly complete your explanation.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This here is the reply of the secretariat of the interior of Kosovska Mitrovica to a cable which was dispatched by the MUP staff in Pristina. The objective being to assess the need for armaments for the reserve police squads, and this is not a document for just Kosovska Mitrovica. This is a document which refers to all the secretariats in the area of Kosovo, its basic purpose being to identify the needs in weapons in order to supply such armaments in a timely fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Quickly, you had said before that there were 58 of these reserve police squads, and you are explaining --

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- The reference to the document for 41 squads. Could you just complete that explanation?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision on the setting up of reserve police squads was adopted in June 1998, and until the 1st of July, 1998, there had been set up 41 police squads. Not all the reserve police squads in all the villages were set up; they were just set up in 41 villages with the remaining balance of 17 villages up to the figure of 58 being set up at a later date.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. The document -- if you look at the first page there, the third sentence, the document purports to summarise, broken down by municipalities the distribution of these weapons. I think you said that the document refers to all of Kosovo. Can you reflect on that. Does this document refer to all of Kosovo or does it refer to your SUP, the requirements for your SUP, Kosovska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not quite clear what your question is. Please, could you repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see it on the screen, in other words, this is the previous document that I've already commented on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you scroll to the top of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this the document dated the 1st of July, 1998?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 284/98.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And it is a document which I've already indicated to you that you had signed, and it deals with the distribution of weapons. Now I think you said that the document refers to the distribution of weapons to the reserve police squad members in all of Kosovo and Metohija. Is that correct or does this document refer to the distribution of weapons in your SUP?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It only refers to the weapons issued in the area of the SUP of Kosovska Mitrovica. I wanted to stress that this was a reply to a cable forwarded to the SUP of Kosovska Mitrovica. It is realistic on my part to assume that such a cable was sent to the other SUPs in Kosovo, not only to the Kosovska Mitrovica one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we just go again to the last page, the text just above the signature block.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The document indicates that the following weapons need to be procured and obtained for the needs of the Kosovska Mitrovica SUP reserve force: Automatic rifles, 800 pieces; semi-automatic rifles, 200 pieces; light machine-guns, 100 pieces, of which there were to be 50 pieces of the M-53 light machine-guns and 50 pieces of M-72 light machine-guns. Were the reserve police squads regularly issued with light machine-guns?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you tell me, please, whether these reserve police squads had an office or a base.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Reserve police squads or RPOs in individual villages were mobilised within the local communes or the villages themselves. As for separate facility for such RPOs, there were none, no purpose-built facilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In that case, when a light machine-gun was issued, where was it kept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All weaponry was issued to individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can I -- what was the policy applied to your knowledge in Kosovo generally and in Kosovska Mitrovica in particular in respect to the arming and employment of volunteers in the police force?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as reservists are concerned, in case of an imminent threat of war and the threat of war, can be included into the units of the Army of Yugoslavia. To be precise, the Army of Yugoslavia in the case of an imminent threat of war or state of war can be brought up to strength by reservists as well.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: By volunteers as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, that possibility does not exist for the Ministry of the Interior. The way it is organised, in terms of all of its units, cannot make use of volunteers. Volunteers can only be used by the Army of Yugoslavia, and such volunteers can be conscripted only through the relevant military bodies. In the area of the Kosovska Mitrovica SUP among the active and reserve police force, there were no volunteers. There were individuals who reported to us who came wishing to join the police, and these were usually the people born in the given area who had moved to other parts of the Republic of Serbia. Once the imminent threat of war and the state of war was declared, they came back to defend their area against terrorist activities and NATO. All such people were sent to the military sector office, and in keeping with the needs of the Army of Yugoslavia they would then be deployed to various VJ units. I know of only one case in the area of Kosovska Mitrovica, it was a person who came to me directly, stating that he wished to join the reserve police force; however, I had to tell him to go to the competent military office, military territorial office, and then subsequently he was made part of a VJ unit. It is the only case that I know of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is important to correct in the transcript that I didn't tell him to go to the military organ or body but to the military territorial organ. It is line 23, page 21. The distinction being a military body as opposed to a military territorial body. We had the witness before who spoke about that, and it is important to distinguish the two in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It probably is resolved by page 22, line 10, which I think is on the same subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I just wanted to draw the attention of the interpreters to that; it is an important issue for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: To summarise what you just said, as a matter of policy is it also your understanding of the law that the police forces could not, and to your knowledge, did not accept people who wanted to volunteer?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What is the policy, to your knowledge, and particularly within your bailiwick of Kosovska Mitrovica, your SUP, with respect to unofficial armed groups or individuals, that is armed groups or individuals that were not attached to any legally established organ but were independent, sometimes referred to as paramilitaries. Did you encounter them; and if so, what was the policy in respect to these people?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the start of the NATO aggression in the area of the Kosovska Mitrovica SUP or, to be more precise, on the road communication Kosovska Mitrovica-Ribarice, there appeared an armed group which was not part of the army or the police. They had modern automatic rifles and wore uniforms. The people who tried to use that road were stopped by the group and valuables were taken. Once notified of their activities - and I was notified by the commander of the police station of Zubin Potok since that locale fell under the jurisdiction of that police station - I ordered that he attend the scene to arrest those men and take them into custody. Once he came there, he couldn't establish any sort of contact with them. They threatened to open fire even at the police. Once I was notified of that by the commander, I advised the head of the MUP staff in Pristina, who undertook measures immediately. As of that moment, the group did not re-appear. As to what happened with them, whether they were sent somewhere, I don't know; however, in the area covered by the Kosovska Mitrovica SUP, those people did not appear again while I was part of that secretariat. Otherwise, the Ministry of the Interior's policy and position as well as the position of the Government of Serbia was that no paramilitary formations are to be allowed. They were not allowed to appear in the area of Kosovo and Metohija. It was said that all means were to be used by the army and police in order to arrest such people and to take them into custody, to surrender them to the competent bodies. First and foremost, measures needed to be taken to prevent them from coming to Kosovo and Metohija, and all roads and other channels of communication were controlled so as to try and prevent it; however, it still happened in Kosovska Mitrovica. It was emphatically addressed, and the unit was sent away, the unit never returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So I take it from your answer that -- and to summarise, that according to the policy of the government and the MUP, as stated, paramilitaries were not to be tolerated; and if the will existed, they could be removed and expelled from the territory of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was until -- or before the 16th of April while I was still head of the secretariat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it your evidence that you only ever received one report in your area of the presence of paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the area under the competence of the secretariat, there was only one group on the road communication between Kosovska Mitrovica and Ribarice. That armed group was removed pursuant to directives received directly from the ministry. I don't know where they went from there, but they never returned to the area of the Kosovska Mitrovica SUP. That is the only group I know of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why did you refer to the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember mentioning the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well -- I'm sorry -- yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Go ahead, I was going to remind him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. You've been interpreted as saying it was until -- or before the 16th of April while I was still head of the secretariat. Now, did something change on the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we turn to the MUP staff. You said yesterday that in June, I think it was, 1998 Sreten Lukic was appointed the head of the MUP staff of Kosovo and Metohija. Can you tell us when that staff was set up, if you know.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a meeting in the MUP staff in Pristina on the 11th of June, 1998. There the assistant minister of the interior informed all heads of secretariats that there were organisational changes within the MUP staff. The new head of the MUP staff in Pristina was Mr. Sreten Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know when the MUP staff of Kosovo and Metohija was originally set up?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you have in mind the MUP staff headed by Mr. Lukic, there was a decision on the formation of that staff dated the 15th of May, 1998. However, the MUP staff was active in Kosovo and Metohija for an extensive period of time and it existed even before 1998 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. What was the role --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: 26 -- I'm sorry, 26, 6, the witness said it existed even before 1990, not 1998. He said "1990."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. I'll ask him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Clarify it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you say the MUP staff for Kosovo and Metohija existed before 1998 or before 1990?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before 1990, except at that time it was called the staff of separate or special units of the police in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What was its role and function in the police organisation in Kosovo in May and June of 1998?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The function of the staff was described in the decision on its formation, which was put into force by the head of the public security department. In the decision inter alia it is stated that the staff is to plan, organise, coordinate, and direct the work of the secretariat of the interior and police border stations in Kosovo and Metohija, especially when it comes to serious security issues and breaches, such as to prevent riots, armed resistance and insurgency, as well as terrorism. There was some other tasks as well. The head of the staff was to report to the head of the public security department concerning his work and the work of the staff. In turn, the head of the public security department was to notify of all the activities on the part of the staff in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do we have that order, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I am not sure. I believe we do or we have documents that relate to that order, but I could give a precise answer after the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If the material is coming at a later stage, that's fine; otherwise, it might be important to get a little more information from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: For example, the date of the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The -- do you remember the date of the decision on the formation of the MUP staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stated that those decisions changed, there were several; however, the decision appointing Mr. Lukic as the staff head dates back to May, or rather, that decision on the formation of the MUP staff in Pristina is dated the 15th of May, 1998. The decision on the appointment of the head as well as the appointment of members of the staff is dated the 11th of June, 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I think this is a suitable time for us to break. We have to break at this stage, Mr. Cvetic. Would you please go with the usher, who will show you where to wait while we have the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall resume at five past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. At the break a question had arisen in respect to the documents that were related to the testimony of the witness. Two of those documents have been located; they are on the exhibit list. They were not listed for this witness. It was intended to use -- to be used with another witness, but they are pretty short documents, and I would ask the leave of the Court to show the witness these documents. One is a document that he refers to in respect to the formation of the staff and its role, and the other one is the -- is the membership of the staff which he said changed from time to time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It sounds as though it would be sensible for us to see these at this stage. Is there any objection to that course? Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Only, Your Honour, if we should know which documents we are going to see because the witness was telling about the documents from May and the 11th of June and whether those documents Mr. Stamp wants to show this witness or some other documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The witness referred to a document of the 15th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Or to a decision of the 15th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I would show the witness the document relevant to that decision. The witness referred to also decisions on the appointment of members of the staff which changed from time to time naturally as perhaps you Judges should know for whatever reason I would show the witness that, and that decision, dated the 5th of -- it is dated for a date in April of 1998. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- date is not clear, but that date would be subsequent to the appointment of the -- of the -- of General Lukic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But does that document have any particular relevance?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The document -- yes, to the extent that it shows the membership of the Joint Command at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, I thought we were talking about the MUP staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- rather than the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we are speaking about the MUP staff for Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I would ask, Your Honour, just to show document 1551 to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you object to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We don't object if we are going to show the witness the document from the 15th of May and the 11th of June as the witness said. The other documents we do not know which documents they are talking about if they are not the documents mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Give us the number of the second one, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The second one is P1552 -- P1252.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, can you have a look at that, Mr. Lukic, yourself and tell me if there's really an objection to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You have to give us some time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, carry on just now, Mr. Stamp, but don't put that document until we get the position clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we have a look and could it be brought up on the screen document 1551 -- Exhibit 1551 -- 15 or 12. Withdrawn. I'm sorry. It is document 1251.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I'd be grateful if we could have the dual screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cvetic, just answer this question yes or no. You see the document on the screen. Is that the document you were referring to earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, can I see the second page of this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This document describes the functions of the joint -- I beg your pardon, of the MUP staff for Kosovo and Metohija, which, as you described, included planning, organising, and coordinating the work of the secretariats and the border police in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. I'd like you to look at paragraph E, and that's on the first page of the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know if I do not know to use this electronic system or we have two documents 1251 and 1252 actually marked as two documents and actually it's one document. So Mr. Stamp is showing to the witness the document I should see first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the one we're looking at at the moment is dated the 15th of May, 1998, to which you've got no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then it's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Carry on, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Among the tasks at E is to training organised units to perform successfully special security assignments and special training for maintaining the readiness of secretariats and organised units, special units of the police, special anti-terrorists units, and mechanised brigades of the police for proceeding according to Kolubara 1. Can you tell us briefly in a sentence or two what is Kolubara 1.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Kolubara 1 plan had been drawn up before I had assumed the post of head of the SUP in Kosovska Mitrovica. It was made by representatives of the army and representatives of the ministry. The basic function of the plan was to define the procedure of organs and units of the police in the event of major civil riots and insurgency or terrorism. Furthermore, the protection of personnel, the protection of facilities, the evacuation of personnel, security, and relocation and work and security at specific places, if that is the location to which the person -- at which the personnel and units of the ministry is not secure enough, so to provide security for such locations. Basically, that is the gist of that plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, the decision refers to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you ask that. Mr. Cvetic, are you surprised to see reference in that passage that was read from the document to special anti-terrorist units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it follows then that special anti-terrorist units fell within the command structure of the MUP staff of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, a distinction needs to be made here in terms of command, namely in respect of the person who is in charge of the unit, that person commands the unit, but that person may not have the right to pass this -- to adopt decisions on the use of the unit in question, to make such decisions. As far as I know, the staff of the MUP in Pristina did not have the authority to make decisions on the use of anti-terrorist units, but if such a decision has been taken, the MUP staff could issue orders to such a unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But in May 1998, who would take the decision to use these units?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the level of the Ministry of the Interior, within the chain of command, the system of command within the Ministry of the Interior, it was solely the minister who could make a decision on the use of a special anti-terrorist unit or a person so empowered by him. And as a rule, that person would be the head of the public security department.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. And you say that that decision having been made by the competent person or body, the MUP staff could issue orders to such a unit. Can we be specific in respect to the JSO, when they were employed for combat manoeuvres in Kosovo would the MUP staff direct their operations while they were employed for combat operations in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the anti-terrorist unit is activated in combat operations, in other words, when such a decision is taken, the head of the MUP staff could issue orders to the commander of that unit. And the commander of that unit would be directly in charge of commanding the unit in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And would that situation apply also to the employment of the SAJ, the OPG, and the PJP when they were engaged in combat manoeuvres in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the JSO units?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I just did. I'm moving on to the SAJ, OPG, and PJP. Well, let's do them one by one. When the PJP was employed or engaged in combat manoeuvres in Kosovo and Metohija, they would also be given directives by the MUP staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The decision on the engagement of the PJPs would be taken at the level of the ministry. According to the same or a similar procedure, as in respect of special anti-terrorist units, the SAJs. And the orders would be submitted to the unit via the MUP staff in Pristina, and the direct command of the units was by the commander of the unit in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, did the -- you said the orders that they would be engaged I think would be submitted by the MUP staff in Pristina. Once they were engaged in Kosovo, did the MUP staff have a role in directing and organising the operations?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. I think that this does not raise from the testimony of this witness, and I think that we had enough leading questions. Like ask the witness the open questions, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I find the question difficult to understand. I think you should try again with that question, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Cvetic, what I'm focusing on is where you said that the orders to engage the units would be submitted to the unit by the MUP staff in Pristina. I'm inquiring as to whether or not the MUP staff would play a role more than just conveying an order to engage the unit. Would the MUP staff be involved in planning and organising the operations of these units once they were engaged in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the MUP staff adopted plans on the use of such units in countering terrorism. In those plans they laid down the basic tasks and the locations at which those units would be engaged. The staff adopted such plans as the staff as a whole, but such plans were also adopted by the Joint Command as of July 1998. As a rule, those plans included the tasks of both the army and the police, and the tasks would be coordinated at the level of the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we focus a little bit now on the Joint Command. You said that sometime in July of 1998 the heads of the SUPs and other senior personnel in the police organisation for Kosovo and Metohija were assembled and were told that a Joint Command would be established. Who announced this to the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm concerned about this. If this is a viva voce examination, you cannot put such questions leading the witness, saying that they assembled and that this and that happened. If you were to follow 94 ter statement, then you would have it right. I think that we are slightly lost in this -- these proceedings. This is in one paragraph, but the Prosecutor is not following that paragraph. So I would like him to ask open questions. Do you know? Or did something happen? The way you put it you have directly told him what he should give you by way of an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Fila, I'm sorry I disagree with you because the witness has already told us that in July 1998 all heads of SUPs were told at a meeting of the MUP staff in Pristina of the Joint Command being set up at the highest level to integrate the activities of the army and the police in the implementation of anti-terrorist operations. So all Mr. Stamp is doing is reminding him of the answer he's given and he's going to ask another question and that's perfectly legitimate. So I repel your objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I apologise. Everything is okay, but the sentences are different. They are being turned around as it were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who made that announcement about the formulation or the formation of the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 10th of July at a meeting in the MUP staff in Pristina attended by all the heads of secretariats, the assistant minister or the head of the public security department - I do not remember exactly which one of the two - told the heads of secretariats that it had been agreed at the highest level to set up a Joint Command for all formations of the army and police to coordinate activities between the army and the police. At this meeting of the MUP staff in Pristina -- at another meeting, rather, on the 22nd of July, 1998, the public security department head informed the meeting that a Joint Command had been set up at the highest level, which Joint Command comprised Nikola Sainovic, Matkovic, Minic, Lukic, Pavkovic, Zoran Andjelkovic, and David Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could you just -- if you just see the names you gave us, tell us the full names and the roles or functions of the persons that you have named. Let's start with Matkovic. What was his full name and what office did he hold?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that his name was Dusko Matkovic and that at that time he was the director of Sartid firm in Smederevo, and that his function in the Joint Command was to promote the work of enterprises in Kosovo and Metohija, that is to revive economic activities, simply speaking, in Kosovo and Metohija. Milomir Minic, and I don't know what his function at the time was, but for a time he had been a prominent official of the SPS, and he held an office in the Federal Assembly, I cannot recall exactly which now. Zoran Andjelkovic was the president of the temporary Executive Council, and in fact in 1998, he was the acting, the ad interim, president of the temporary Executive Council and was elected to the post of president of the temporary Executive Council at the end of 1998. Mr. Pavkovic was the commander of the Pristina Corps, and David Gajic was the person in charge of the coordination of the work of the State Security Service in Kosovo and Metohija, otherwise he was the assistant of the head of the state security department. Mr. Nikola Sainovic at the time was the vice premier of the federal government.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you said Lukic, by that I take it you mean General Lukic, head of the Kosovo MUP staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, according to this decision on appointment, he -- on the appointment of heads and members of the staff, he was the head of the Pristina staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you remember if General Pavkovic was the only military personnel who was a member of the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it was notified.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know who was the head of the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The head of the Joint Command was Nikola Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you were indicating that after its establishment, the organisation and direction of the various units in the field in Kosovo, the police units and the VJ units, was done by the Joint Command. They were responsible for planning, organising, and directing the coordinated activities of these various military and police units in the field in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is an exceptionally leading question. The witness precisely said that the Joint Command was formed in order to coordinate activities between the army and the police. These were his words, and now we have planning and everything else enumerated by Mr. Stamp in his leading question. I ask for this to be redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, what do you have to say on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think I was quoting -- well, not quoting directly because I can't find it. I think I was summarising the sense of what the witness was saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I think you went much further than what has been said so far by the witness, and therefore I sustain that objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In respect to operations of police units and VJ units in the field in Kosovo, did the Joint Command have any role and functions in respect to those operations?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What was the role of the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Joint Command adopted plans, or rather, issued orders on the activation of units to suppress terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija. They issued orders and decisions. It was all done and verified by the Joint Command. They included tasks issued to units, to the units engaged in the given operation. A plan had to be verified by the Joint Command, and as such it was forwarded to the unit commanders, commanders of those units which were planned as a part of that action or activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What was the arrangement made or what was the -- what effectively was the relationship between the Joint Command once it had been established and the MUP staff for Kosovo and Metohija? Here you have two governing bodies, if I may put it that way. How did they regulate their relationship, do you know?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The head of the staff was a member of the Joint Command. As for the tasks discussed at the Joint Command, he was the person implementing those tasks via the staff. And then, in return, he would report on the activities of the staff to the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you ever attend a meeting -- any meeting of the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, I take it that there would have been meetings of the MUP staff for Kosovo and Metohija and senior MUP personnel in Kosovo and Metohija. Did you, as the head of a SUP for Kosovska Mitrovica, attend these meetings?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How frequent were these meetings, can you recall?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule, at least once a month; and if needed, more frequently. For example, during 1999 I attended six meetings of the MUP staff at Pristina; these were on the 17th of February, on the 8th of March, the 17th of March, the 29th of March, the 4th of April, and the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could the witness -- or could we bring up Exhibit P1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This document, sir, is the minutes of the meeting of the police leadership in Kosovo and Metohija for the 4th of April, 1999. If you look near the bottom of the first page, do you see that you attended that meeting? It records you attending as the chief of the Kosovska Mitrovica secretariat.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And at this meeting -- or this document indicates that at this meeting the various chiefs of SUPs gave reports on the situation in their areas. Is that something that would happen at these meetings?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think I have to try to move quickly because of time, and I think it would be speedier if I just handed him a copy. I don't know if I could be permitted to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you have to take the time you require when matters are important. It's for you, I think, to judge the importance of what you're doing. I have no objection to you handing hard copies of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we scroll to the next page of this document and perhaps if we just focus on the English document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You will see, Mr. Cvetic, that present also at the meeting were the various PJP detachment commanders who gave reports on their activities. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You will see also that present and reporting were the heads of the SAJ units and the JSO commander, who was also reported on what they were doing. That's page 3 to 4 of your document -- of the copy in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But as for Milorad Jankovic, commander of the JSO, I don't know that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Also in the meeting you can see from this document was General Sreten Lukic and Mr. Obrad Stevanovic, who was assistant minister at the time. That would be on page 4, I think, of your document.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before we move from that page, it says here that among the taskings that General Lukic discussed and issued was obligatory reporting of chiefs of secretariats and unit commanders to the staff. Can you comment on this, how frequently were you required to report on the activities of the units and your SUPs up the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that -- sorry, Your Honour. I think that we have one translation problem here. I'm not objecting to Mr. Stamp not understanding it, but here in the original B/C/S version doesn't say "reporting." The word is "javljanje" so the translators can maybe translate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do you say it is?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Calling. It doesn't say reporting, just calling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we better have the passage read, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you find, Mr. Cvetic, the section where General Lukic was issuing tasks, and the last task that he spoke of immediately before the section of Obrad Stevanovic, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's the last line on the third page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, learned counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm just going to ask you when you find it to read it aloud.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if I could ask the translators to translate it from what the witness reads and not from the document that they have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are we on the correct page, Mr. -- Sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The last line of page 3 on your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are we on the correct page? We are.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's the previous page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- one page before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the last line now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 3, item 2, last line: "Mandatory calling in of SUP chiefs and unit commanders to the staff." Yes, they had the duty to call in on a daily basis the heads of the SUPs, and if needed they had to do that more frequently. All SUPs in the area of Kosovo and Metohija forwarded daily reports on the current events in their respective areas. These were reported to the MUP staff in Pristina. Apart from that, every morning each of the SUP chiefs had to call the MUP staff head in Pristina between 8.00 and 8.30 to report on the latest events, rather, to brief him on any events which may be of interest and had not been encompassed in the daily report of the previous day. Such information or such reports were forwarded at 4.00 or 5.00 a.m., and in that period between 4.00 and 8.00 a.m., they were supposed to report on any events which may have occurred, particularly if they were of security concern and had not been made part of the daily report sent to the MUP staff in Pristina. The MUP staff in Pristina also forwarded reports to the SUPs on the current events by way of daily briefs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the reports that you said -- the daily reports that were forwarded, these reports were in -- well, in what form were these daily reports that were forwarded? Were they written or oral?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Daily reports were done by phone or through telephone telegraph communication links; however, all SUPs had special telephone lines in Kosovo. We used to refer to that line as "specijal" and we used it to contact the staff head. Provided he was away or busy, then the contact would be made with the deputy staff head.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we scroll to the last page. It says on the last page here that "federal deputy prime minister Nikola Sainovic joined the work, pointing to the need of ending the first phase of anti-terrorist operations today in order to ensure active defence and protection of the territory and protection of the border against the aggressor's potential penetration of the enemy into the depth of the FRY. He also stressed that persons being detained on account of perpetrating crimes are to be held until such time as they are taken over by judicial organs."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you remember Mr. Sainovic attending that meeting?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Sainovic attended that meeting. At that meeting, Mr. Sainovic assisted, requested, and asked all those present for the police to conduct themselves highly professionally when carrying out their duties, to be strict within anyone committing any sort of misdemeanour or crime. He said that such individuals should be taken into custody and kept there until wartime military courts are set up, and the measures were being undertaken to establish such courts at the time. Apart from that, he pointed out that all operations that had been planned to take place on -- up until -- up to the 4th of April to be concluded by the end of that day and to move on to the other two tasks. The first one was to protect the given unit at the positions -- at the last positions they attained. It meant that they were to make trenches and camouflage themselves against any NATO attacks. The second task was to secure and protect the border so as to prevent NATO land forces from coming in. All activities are to be planned and carried out together with the Army of Yugoslavia, and those individuals which excelled in the operations until then should be nominated for promotion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was the -- well, before I ask the question just to go back to something you answered. While you were in Kosovo up to the 20th of April, 1999, were any of these wartime courts established? Do you know of them being established?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the meetings -- in the meetings at the staff I was told that measures were taken in order to train the personnel of military courts and to set them up. I am not familiar as to the training, but all reports about individual offenders were forwarded, instead, to the regular courts which were operational at the time in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, page 45, line 14: Military war courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was this the only meeting that you attended that Mr. Sainovic was present at, or were there any other meeting or meetings?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. I don't know what year you have in mind. If you have in mind 1999, that was the only meeting that I attended when I saw Mr. Sainovic and the only one where he participated in the meeting. He took part in the discussion. He was also present at the meeting on the 29th of March, 1999, which was held in the basement of the Grand, but there he did not take any part in discussion. He observed, together with the assistant minister, and listened to the report on NATO attacks against the FRY and he was also interested to learn about the public opinion and the reaction of the media.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, page 46, line 5, the report of agencies on NATO attacks; that is what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp. Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour, another correction. Page 46, line 1, in the transcript we have: "He took part in the discussion," whereas the witness, he said he did not take part in the discussion, that he was only present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I don't think that's correct. That reference is to the earlier meeting. The witness goes on to say on the 29th of March he did not take any part. Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's turn to operations in the field during 1999. I understand from your testimony that at that time the operation in the field, the directives for those operations in the field were issued by the Joint Command. Do you know how these orders were transmitted, in what form?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we bring up P1968, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know, orders, as prescribed, were issued as directives, commands, or orders and decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'd like to -- well --

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
