utterances.text: Yes, this is one of the orders, and it is called a zapovest.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Which also translates in English as order, interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is an order dated the 24th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we look quickly at the last page of the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, my first question is: While you were in Kosovo, had you seen orders of a Joint Command that resemble this order before; and secondly -- well, could you answer the first question first. Does this order resemble orders you had seen while you were exercising command function in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is a uniform methodology for drawing up orders which has been prescribed and which is applicable to all situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In the block at the right at the bottom of the -- at the end of the order, it just has Joint Command for KiM. There is no signature or person identified there. Was that a common thing or is that unusual?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For what I had occasion to see, it was customary.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could go back to the first page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The document immediately under the word "order" refers to operations to defeat Siptar terrorist forces in the Drenica region. Firstly, was -- Drenica was a region a part of the jurisdiction or within the territorial jurisdiction of the Kosovska Mitrovica SUP?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for Drenicas, there is a river Drenica, there is a mountain Drenica, and there is a Drenica region in Kosovo. The Drenica region encompasses the area in the triangle between Srbica, Glina, and Glogovac in the geographical sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So I take it that geographically it was within the territorial area of your SUP?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A part of Drenica is in the geographical area of the SUP of Kosovska Mitrovica as well as in the areas of other secretariats. But the focus is on the area of Srbica. And when one says "Drenica," one usually has Srbica in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. The order speaks for itself, and you have seen it recently. It makes provision for the support -- or for coordinating the activities of various units in an operation in Drenica. Could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we move to page 2 of that document, the top of page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And we see an item number 2 at the top of that page. That is in -- that is at the bottom of page 2 of the English version of the translation. And I read it: "The Pristina Corps with reinforcements and the armed non-Siptar population in KiM," Kosovo and Metohija, "shall support MUP forces in defeating and destroying the STS in the zone of responsibility." The Pristina Corps was acting in coordination with MUP forces or in support of MUP forces, and acting with them was armed non-Siptar population. What do you understand that expression to mean "armed non-Siptar population" in the context of this order?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unarmed -- armed, sorry, non-Siptar population I think, most probably, means the Serb population. Most probably assigned to reserve police squads. I don't know what a person -- who was the person who drew up or participated in the drawing up of this order meant by it. Most probably, the Serbian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you said most probably members of the reserve police squad. Your answer "most probably," is that based on your experience and knowledge of the use and employment of the reserve police squads in Kosovo at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Still calls for speculation. And the witness said "most probably," but of course he cannot be sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think your question should have been an open question, asking him the basis for his --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- View.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: On what basis, sir, do you say that the armed non-Siptar population referred to here was most probably members of the reserve police squads?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire Serbian population that was in the area, it was armed, and a part of that population was assigned to reserve police squads and another part also to units of the Army of Yugoslavia, that is the military territorial units. Therefore, most probably this refers to the Serbian population, to Serbs. For, in the area of Drenica, the majority population was Albanian and there was a small percentage of Serbs there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In your earlier answer you did refer specifically to the reserve police squads, but now you refer also to the military territorial units. Are you suggesting that both of them fall within the expression "armed non-Siptar population"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In practice, when a task had to be undertaken, what, in your experience, was the working relationship between the reserve police squads and the regular police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The regular police planned the missions, and as part of those tasks it also assigned its tasks to the reserve police squads and linked with them, liaised with them. The reserve police squads were as a rule were squads tasked with a defence of inhabited places, but in the zone of combat operations where there participated units of the army and units of the police, the population of the area would also join in, it would also join the units in carrying out the planned tasks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we look briefly at P1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This again is -- is a record of a meeting of the ministry staff dated the 21st of December, 1998. If you could look at page 2, I think it is of -- of the document, you see a reference there to the implementation of the Milosevic-Holbrooke agreement. Do you see that? Can you find it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm informed it's the -- it's on the first page, the penultimate paragraph of the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we return to the first page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you read the last paragraph -- the last two paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'll read the last sentence. "The OSCE mission should be told where there are terrorists and if they cannot do anything, we should tell them the police will. According to the Agreement, we should not allow them access to any military or police facility." Were you instructed by the persons in charge of the MUP to prevent the OSCE mission members from entering into police and military facilities?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, I had at least ten meetings with the OSCE mission which was in the area of Kosovo and Metohija, and those meetings took place in my office.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. The document says: "We should not allow them access to any military or police facility." What did you understand those instructions to mean?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you -- are we on the first page of the document? It's on the last paragraph of the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you see that now?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We had General DZ yesterday here, and we saw that there is some misunderstandings regarding this issue in between OSCE mission in Kosovo and Serbian authorities. And to ask this witness how did he understood this message would be speculative. Or in fairness to this witness that agreement should be shown to him and see if there is in that agreement anything that should permit this mission to inspect the depots, army depots or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, that's not the issue that's being explored, it's not the interpretation of the agreement that's being explored; if it were, you would be right. But in this instance what Mr. Stamp is exploring how this was given effect to, that's all. This is the minute of a meeting the witness was at, and that's all he was asking him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Otherwise we all can read the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We can, but that's not -- that doesn't tell us whether anything was done about it. So carry on, please, Mr. Stamp. Ask the question again. I think the witness has probably forgotten it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The instructions from the minister Stojiljkovic was: "We should not allow them access to any military or police facility." What --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise for slowing you down, but this is of the essence. The entire sentence should be read and the entire sentence says: "According to the Agreement, we should not allow them access." So it means according to the agreement that is not their obligation, and that is how that is to be interpreted in our language. So it is according to the agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's the -- that's the point I've just ruled on. That's immaterial to the questions that are being asked of this witness, and please don't interrupt on that basis again when a ruling has already been made. All that's being sought is an explanation of what in fact happened here. Now, please ask the question, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you're told that we should not allow the OSCE mission any access to any military or police facility what did you understand that to mean and what was done about this order?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The members of the OSCE mission who were in the area of Kosovska Mitrovica, they did not go into the warehouses, the depots of the police armaments, but they did come for talks, to see me as the head of the police as well as to talk with my immediate associates. Our position was that we were to accept the OSCE mission and to present everything that we had to them in order for the real truth to be ascertained as to who was it in Kosovo that wanted peace and negotiated a peaceful solution and who did not. Who whatever we had at our disposal, we submitted to the OSCE mission. I don't know that any of the members of the OSCE in the area of Kosovska Mitrovica demanded access to depots of armaments available to the police. It was stated at the meeting that we should receive, accept, the OSCE mission, take it in, but should not allow them entry into certain zones where they can come to harm or be threatened, where there were operations being carried out because of their own security considerations. As for the entering into depots, I don't know about that. There were no such demands by the OSCE. In addition to the mission of the OSCE in Kosovska Mitrovica, we also had the K diplomatic mission and we pursued excellent cooperation with them; they came to see us, we went to see them, and we did many jobs together and in agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, is this a suitable point to interrupt you?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. We have to interrupt again and have a break, Mr. Cvetic, so could you please leave again with the usher, and we'll see you again at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that the OSCE mission members were not allowed to enter the depots. How about police barracks, what was the situation in respect to those? Were they or were they not allowed to enter police barracks?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Meaning they were not?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The information we received was that it was a verifying mission. They were there to ascertain what the situation was and what was being done by the Ministry of the Interior on one side and by -- what was done by the terrorists on the other side. We were told that it was not a control-type mission which would be able to control the work of the secretariats of the interior. We didn't have to report to them or anything of that nature. That was the position at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour, for interrupting at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But maybe it should be clarified with the witness whether police had barracks or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're asking ourselves that question and anticipate that it would be cleared up later.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did the police have any housing facilities for the units that we were discussing earlier or any police units that were brought into the area or -- withdrawn. Did the police have any housing facilities, any facilities at all to house policemen, at the police stations?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the 1990s, in the Army of Yugoslavia barracks, in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, there were buildings erected in order to accommodate police units, which were engaged in operations in Kosovo and Metohija. They were used as accommodation and they kept their weaponry there as well, which they brought with them once they had been mobilised prior to entering Kosovo. Such buildings did not exist in each and every barracks. I remember them being in Kosovska Mitrovica and in Pec in the barracks there, and I know that for a fact because I saw them personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we have a look quickly at P2528.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is an order dated the 21st of October, 1998, and if we look at the second page, in the signature block of the second page, we can see that it's signed by Major-General Sreten Lukic. That's correct? You see that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, but this document was not signed by Sreten Lukic. It is another person's signature, although his name was typed out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So -- but the document was issued by the ministry staff of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Quickly if we could return to the first page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I'll just read --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we scroll down to that item 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You could probably follow in Serbian while I read the section in English. "At check-points and other places where the police work, contact with the mission members may be made only by the police members designated for this at each check-point. They will allow mission members, without the obligation of advanced notification, to monitor and record police work at all work places without entering work and accommodation facilities and training grounds" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would Mr. Stamp please read slowly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: "Without entering work places -- work and accommodation facilities and training grounds, except for facilities in SUP, OUP, and police station headquarters when they are establishing official contacts or submitting requests for such contacts."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Does that order reflect what actually took place on the ground in Kosovska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we look at the next page in the Serbian version, and it's -- we can stay on the same page in the English version for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And in respect to -- you have a section here entitled "reporting and informing." "Urgent and daily reports submitted to previously order mentioned measures on details on the following occurrences and events: 1, terrorist actions," and it lists the type of actions and goes on. "2, police operations carried out, the type of operations, the time and place of operation, the number of police members participating in the operation, combat and noncombat equipment, and vehicles and so on, and the results and consequences." Did the various SUPs and OUP comply with that order to report in that manner?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was drafted by the MUP staff in Pristina prescribing a uniform methodology to be used across all the secretariats. All the secretariats were duty-bound to follow the methodology and to inform the staff pursuant to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There's just one thing I want to clarify before I move on. Were all the reporting -- was the reporting up from the OUP to the SUP and from the SUP to the ministry in Belgrade and to the MUP for Kosovo and Metohija, was it always orally or sometimes orally and sometimes in writing?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This type of briefing or reporting based on this document issued by the MUP Pristina staff was forwarded to all police stations and OUPs within the respective SUPs. All police stations and OUPs had to brief the secretariat on the topics mentioned. Based on that, the secretariats compiled information which would then be forwarded to the MUP staff in Pristina. For example, a report of a police station or an OUP would not be drafted unless they had issues to address, mentioned here. Otherwise they would simply report to their superior that there were no provocations, no terrorist attacks, and there were no planned or carried out police activities. Otherwise, they were duty-bound to report following this methodology, and it included the whole chain down from the police stations via the OUPs, SUPs, up to the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And when the reports were made, some of these reports were in writing and some were made orally?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually in written form.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we look at P1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: P1990 are minutes of the meeting of the MUP staff of the 17th of February, 1999, in February. And you can see on the first page there that General Sreten Lukic opened the meeting which was devoted to the security situation and assigning tasks. And also present was the public security department chief, General Djordjevic, and the minister Vlajko Stojiljkovic. I'd like you to look at the last page of this document. It is a record of the instructions of the minister, and it says in one item that you were to approach and engage volunteers carefully, linking their engagement through the reserve police force when assessed as necessary.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't see this in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we go back to the bottom of the previous page. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you comment on that, because my understanding from what you had said before was that it was not the policy and it was also not lawful for the police to engage volunteers. And here the minutes indicate that the minister said that you should approach and engage volunteers carefully, linking their engagement through the reserve police force when assessed as necessary.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pursuant to the law on the Army of Yugoslavia, I believe in Article 15 it is envisaged that the Army of Yugoslavia, in case of an imminent threat of war and state of war, may be manned by volunteers. Therefore, the legislator did not allow for such a possibility to any other defence structures to be able to make use of volunteers, including the Ministry of the Interior. What is stated here by the minister runs contrary to the existing legislation at the time. At the meeting at the MUP staff in Pristina, which was also held -- I apologise. Which was held on the 17th of March, the head of the MUP staff in Pristina, inter alia, raised the issue of volunteers. He stated that in case volunteers appeared in the area of Kosovo and Metohija, such men are to be retained in those locations. And once war operations begin, the volunteers were to be included in the MUP system. This was also illegally and still is. However, there is a difference between volunteers and paramilitary formations. Volunteers were individuals appearing in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, whereas paramilitary formations were units with their own komandir or komandant. They were uniformed and carried arms. As I stated, only one such unit as I know appeared in the territory of the Kosovska Mitrovica SUP. And thanks to an energetic measure taken by the SUP, the unit was driven out. I know of no other paramilitary units within the territory of the Kosovska Mitrovica SUP while I was chief of the SUP, or rather, until the 16th of April. After the 16th of April, I have no knowledge what took place. Otherwise, my answer would be either the person drafting this was not familiar with the law or the intention was such but I can only speculate as to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... He repeated now but it was not entered in the transcript that it was an energetic measure taken by the MUP staff and here we have S-U-P, SUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. A number of points for clarification from that. You've again referred to the 16th of April which I asked you before. What is the significance of the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. I didn't understand your question. On the 16th of April I was dismissed from my duty as the head of SUP at the staff meeting in Pristina. As of that moment, I was no longer chief of the Kosovska Mitrovica SUP. Another person was appointed to that position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yesterday you told us that that was the 28th of April.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. On the 28th of April, I left the territory of Kosovo. Between the 16th of April, when I was relieved -- or to be more precise, there was a decision on the appointment of the new head of the Kosovska Mitrovica SUP is dated the 15th of April. Therefore, formally speaking, as of April 15th I was no longer head of the Kosovska Mitrovica SUP; however, I was informed of this at the staff MUP meeting in Kosovska Mitrovica on the 16th of April. Between that day and the 30th, as was stated in the decision, I stayed with the Kosovska Mitrovica SUP to hand over my duties to the newly appointed chief. I handed over my duties completely on the 20th of April, and I left the territory of Kosovska Mitrovica on the 28th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the decision --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you. Were you -- did you leave your post voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was sent to Kosovo and Metohija after having been dismissed from the duty as the chief of SUP in Kragujevac pursuant to the order of the then-deputy minister of the interior, Mr. Radovan Stojicic, a.k.a. Badza. A decision was issued on the 1st of January, 1997, however, I was only sent on the 16th of December, 1997, to a new position. According to the decision I remained there until the 30th of April, 1999. In true fact, I was dismissed on the 16th of April and left Kosovo on the 28th of April. Pursuant to the law on internal affairs people can be sent to carry out tasks to other secretariats as envisaged in Article 72 on the law of internal affairs. In that article among other things it is stated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think I need to know any more about that. You continued to serve in the police until the 30th of March, 2006?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, yesterday I noted that you retired from the police force on the 30th of March, 2006. Was that a mistake?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I was retired on the 30th of March this year, I retired from the police, but upon return from Kosovo for two and a half months I was not assigned anywhere, I was on my leave. On the 12th of June, on orders of the head of the public security department, I was seconded to the federal ministry for refugees, displaced persons, and humanitarian aid. I stayed with the federal ministry until it was disbanded --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the end of December --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's enough for me, thank you. And one final question on the main answer you were giving you said -- made a reference to the head of the MUP staff. Was that a reference to Mr. Lukic? The person who said that the volunteers should not be released but should be retained and then engaged if a state of war followed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Returning to that document, just one item on it before we leave. On the last page we see here that you were enjoined to raise disciplined behaviour and appearance of policemen to a higher level, do away with Rambo-style caps and bandannas. Up until that period -- or withdrawn. Was it your experience that sometimes police officers dressed in Rambo-style caps and bandannas?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were individual police members who wore hats, bandannas, or the so-called Rambo caps, as stated in the minutes, but these were individual cases. At all meetings at the MUP staff in Pristina and in the seat of the MUP in Belgrade, it was always emphasised that the police should wear uniforms in keeping with the rule book and that all other parts of uniform not -- all other parts of uniform and equipment not envisaged in the rule book may not be used. Against individuals from the police who insist on wearing such items, disciplinary measures are to be undertaken because they've committed a breach of their police duties. However, there were policemen who sported such items.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This must have been a major problem if it arose at every meeting in Pristina and Belgrade. How on earth could you not control the basic uniform that policemen wore?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The policemen had three types of uniform: Dress uniform, work uniform, and the intervention uniform, as it was called. The problem did not exist only in the area of Kosovo but in other secretariats as well. Some people wore different items or they were unbuttoned, they did not wear the proper hat, and measures were taken against such individuals. There were such individuals in Kosovo who sported hats and bandannas in far greater numbers than in the areas of other secretariats in Serbia. As for the lack of discipline with the police members, well, that existed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not it was required that the MUP staff in Pristina report on police activities to the MUP headquarters in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the decision on the formation of the MUP staff in Pristina, among other things, we find that the head of the MUP staff in Pristina is to inform the head of the public security department as regards his work and the work of the staff. The seat of the public security department was in Belgrade. The head of the department used to come to Kosovo on occasion, and then he would receive information there. However, when he was absent from Kosovo, information was sent to Belgrade. Concerning the work of the MUP staff in Kosovo, not only the head of the department was to be informed but also the minister of the interior. Information was forwarded directly to the top of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we bring up P1100.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is a report to the Ministry of the Interior in Belgrade of the 27th of March, 1999, and it purports to -- to be a summary of events and occurrences and information of importance for security, registered in the period of 0600 hours on the 27th of March to 0600 hours on the 28th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we just have a look at the end of this document, please, at the signature block.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you see who signed it or on whose behalf it is signed.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is signed on behalf of the head of the staff, Major-General Sreten Lukic and whose signature it is I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think for this one, with leave of the Court, I have to hand you a copy. Because you have to look through -- I know you have seen it recently, but I would like you to look through it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we could go back to the first page -- or the second page of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if you could follow with me as I run through the document quickly. So let's have the English version. It refers to attacks by NATO armed forces, and in the several paragraphs it discusses and reports upon attacks in various municipalities in Kosovo and Metohija. It continues discussing these attacks, not only attacks of NATO forces but attacks by persons described as terrorists on the 25th, 26th of March in several, if not all, of the municipalities of Kosovo. And we come to the end of the document at item 5 it says: "Serious crimes committed" -- are we there?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we -- if I could ask the usher to follow with the English document alone. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And it refers to an event on the 26th of March where persons were caught -- 21 persons were caught committing the act of theft, and this was in Pristina. And refers to another incident in Djakovica where 17 persons were caught engaged in the act of aggravated theft. Mr. Cvetic, we have heard persons in this court say that on the 24th, 25th, 26th of March in various places in Kosovo, I gave you two examples, in Suva Reka on the 25th of March, in Podujevo on the 26th of March, police personnel were involved in the killings of dozens of civilians. Is there any explanation you could offer as to why events of that nature are not reflected in the report sent up to the ministry in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This methodology of writing reports is uniform, applied from the SUP and through the staff up to the ministry. I have stated that the head of the staff reported to the head of the public security department and the minister, and here it can be seen that he also informs others as well. I cannot say because I have no knowledge whatsoever, why this report does not describe those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. If I may return briefly to the operations in the field when the various units of the MUP were involved in operations in Kosovo. Would they -- what role, generally speaking, would the regular police attached to the SUPs play in those operations? For example, we saw an operation that was ordered by the Joint Command earlier today. What would be the role of your regular police personnel in your SUP?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the role of the regular police of the SUP was to secure or to ensure accommodation and food, in other words, all the logistical requirements, to use a military terminology, the rear support for the units in question. Otherwise, the regular police in the secretariats worked on patrol and beat duties, on securing road communications, check-points, and similar. As -- and securing facilities of importance such as water-supply lines, dairies, bakeries, institutions of the system of organs of authority, that was done by the regular police. Regular police that was not part of the PJPs did not take part in combat operations. In combat operations, in suppressing anti-terrorist units participated the PJPs, the special operation units, and the special anti-terrorist units. That was envisaged in the plan of the command in orders issued by the command as orders proper or as directives or instructions. In the zone of responsibility of those units, if there should be found other units such as reserve police squads or regular police units, if they happened to be in the area they, too, will have specific tasks. But as for their direct participation, there was none of that, apart from the use of these units, because they were both trained and equipped for such purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You told us that policemen had three types of uniform, and one of them was described by you as an intervention uniform. What does intervention mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These were uniforms worn by the PJP, the special anti-terrorist unit members, those were the uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And in what way did they differ from a working uniform --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In what way did they differ from the working uniform of a policeman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were different in colour. I'm not quite sure how to explain it -- actually, what it is, it is a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but you said --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the working uniform of the police was also a camouflage uniform, but it was in a different colour. The police uniform was blue, and the intervention units uniform was in the olive-drab hue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did the -- or may I just show you a document since --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we have a look at 1249. P1249 I should -- I'm sorry. P1052.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very briefly, during your tenure in Kosovska Mitrovica, were you familiar with documents like that; and can you tell us, if so, what this document is?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were documents like this. There were similar documents. This is the plan of work of radio stations. Then there were documents about the plan of the maintenance of the communications system during operations and similar. Otherwise, the designations used in this document, i.e., the call signals which are indicated in this document, well, as regards those I am familiar with some of those call signals.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Have a look at the document; it is undated. Can you say about when this document would have been current if you look at the call signal codes on page 2. Can you give us an approximate date for the -- when this document was in effect?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was current in 1998 or 1999 or both 1998 and 1999, given the fact that certain designations from this document feature in both years, 1998 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You see on the first page item 1 refers to the call signal for the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with this call signal for the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. But you see some codes for call signals. Are you familiar with any of them that you see there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Which ones are you familiar with?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the Iber-40 call signal, the Osa-1, these two call signals.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The first call signal is Ibar, I-b-a-r, dash 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What does Ibar-40 indicate?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ibar-40, that was the call signal of the commander of the 125th Motorised Brigade from Kosovska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. And we can see that on the -- in the same row on the corresponding column -- if you look on the right-hand side of your screen do you see some other call signal codes? Do you see near the bottom one Cegar-1? Do you know what that refers to?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Which unit is that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the call signal for the commander of the 37th Detachment of the PJPs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That was from where, firstly?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is from the SUP of Nis.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And it was commanded by whom? Do you know the name of the commander of that unit?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember the first -- recall the first name, but the last name I can. The commander of that unit was Colonel Mitrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So I take it that these units were all integrated into one communications scheme?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you know about an event on the 26th of March at Izbica in your -- your -- within the jurisdiction of your SUP in which dozens of persons were killed allegedly by security forces of the FRY?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was the head of the SUP in Kosovska Mitrovica, I had not heard about that event, nor had anybody informed me about that event. Nothing was mentioned about that event at that time, otherwise in the area they were operating numerous units, both the Army of Yugoslavia and the police. I can enumerate of the units of the Army of Yugoslavia that were in the area at the time when the NATO aggression started on the 24th of March, that is, the 7th Infantry Brigade arrived there from Krusevac as well as the 37th Infantry Brigade from Raska. The commanders of these brigades were Dikovic and Cirkovic, I think, and the PJPs were at there as well as the special units of the police, the special operations unit, and the operations sweep groups were also working there. For a while, the 125th Motorised Brigade unit was there in the area also. Later, according to the plan of combat use, it left for another area. Then there were also active from other parts, from other secretariats, other units, not only PJPs, not only the PJPs that were physically located in Kosovska Mitrovica but also PJP units that were from the areas of Pec. And in that area there were also PJPs from Belgrade and from Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If and when serious crimes were committed by police officers - and when I say "serious crimes," I mean crimes of the nature of murder, arson, and expulsion of people from their homes or communities - when those crimes were committed, what was the responsibility of the police command in respect to perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That person should have been arrested, first and foremost.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And when --

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And with a proper criminal complaint handed over to the competent court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, do you know how many, if any, criminal complaints were handed over to competent courts in Kosovo and Metohija while you were there in respect to allegations of murder, arson, and acts of expulsion against police officers in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I don't know that there were any of those. As for breaches of discipline on the part of the police, yes, we did have that. There was theft, there was looting, there was arson. I don't know how many of those cases had been referred to courts. I think, this is just my view, that these events just boiled down to the pronouncement that we should elevate the level of discipline, that the policemen should perform their duties professionally, and also that no energetic steps were taken at the time. In other words, I don't know that any were taken. Otherwise, in the area of the Kosovska Mitrovica SUP on account of the occurrence of different thefts and aggravating thefts, criminal complaints were indeed filed against individuals, also on account of thefts of motor vehicles criminal complaints were filed, but not against members of the police, that is to say I don't know of any such complaints against members of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What I'm asking - and this is my last question really - is: As the head of a SUP, and you normally attended these meetings of the staff for the entire police of Kosovo, do you know of police officers being charged for murder of Kosovar Albanians, arson of Kosovar Albanian property, expulsion of Kosovar Albanians from their homes at the time when you were there? Do you know of that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: One moment, I think I've lost translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm terribly sorry. I forgot to switch on my microphone. The interpreter, yes, will repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was in the area of the SUP of Kosovska Mitrovica, I had no such information whatsoever, but when I returned from Kosovska Mitrovica, quite a bit later, in fact, that was, I believe, in the year 2005, I heard -- actually, I saw in the papers and the mass media, I -- about the -- I was informed about the incident in Suva Reka. And the proceedings were instituted before the war crimes tribunal, its special chapter in Belgrade, against the commander and the members of the 37th Detachment of the PJP.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President, Your Honours, for the additional time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Cvetic, that concludes the proceedings for today, and it concludes the examination by the Prosecution. There are further counsel to ask questions for the accused, that will be tomorrow. And we'll resume at 2.15 tomorrow. Just give me a moment to check which courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So we will actually be in Courtroom I, the courtroom you were in yesterday, at 2.15 tomorrow. Meanwhile, I remind you again not to discuss the evidence with anyone at all, and come back here having thought about and discussed other things overnight and we'll see you at 2.15 tomorrow. Please now leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan, on the question of Sterenberg and whether he will be a possibility next week. You were going to tell me about two hours ago, but I forgot and perhaps you did also.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we are opposed to having the witness testify next week -- or at least we're opposed to having to cross-examine him next week. We've -- we're not opposed to his direct examination. The reasons we're opposed to cross-examination are the following. This witness is for all intents and purposes an expert. He's -- his expertise is reflected in the disclosure, and the reason we we're not prepared to cross-examine him is because of the volume of that disclosure, which grew again this evening. And briefly in November --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You actually don't need to go further because I did indicate to you if on your own responsibility you told us that it would not be appropriate for the cross-examination -- or at least for the witness to give evidence, then we would accept that -- at least evidence at this time we would accept that. And we are grateful for the concession that his examination-in-chief can take place next week. So what will happen is the decision will be filed tomorrow making the position clear. I can tell you that all the submissions of the Prosecution, at least the effect will be given to the relief they seek, except in relation to the Rule 70 witness. And therefore, I think that increases the witness list by perhaps one once the withdrawn witnesses are deleted. But the specific terms of that decision will be filed tomorrow. Mr. Stamp, I take it that what will happen in these circumstances is that Sterenberg will give his direct evidence on Monday?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I guess it's probably too late to mention anything that would result in a debate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You were going to bring him in now, were you?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. We'll take the direct on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So we're adjourned now to Courtroom II at 2.15 tomorrow -- Courtroom I at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 8th day of December, 2006, at 2.15 p.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
